key_facts: **Intertrigo** is inflammation of skin folds from friction, heat and moisture; it is a pattern, not one disease.
Breasts, groin, axillae, abdominal folds, between toes; obesity, diabetes, incontinence and hot weather predispose.
Look for secondary *Candida* (satellite papules), dermatophyte (active edge), **erythrasma** (coral-red Wood's light) or streptococcus.
Keep folds dry, reduce friction, barrier paste; hydrocortisone 1% for 1–2 weeks; topical azole if candida likely.
Persistent flexural rashes: think inverse psoriasis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, contact allergy, Hailey–Hailey or extramammary Paget's.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: Superficial **inflammation of opposed skin surfaces** (flexures/folds) driven by heat, moisture, friction, and poor evaporation. May be purely irritant or complicated by yeast/bacteria; often overlaps inflammatory dermatoses (psoriasis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, contact allergy).

sub: Any age; common in obesity, diabetes, immobility, incontinence and infants (napkin and neck folds).

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: Occluded flexures trap sweat → maceration → barrier failure → inflammation ± overgrowth of resident flora (*Candida*, Corynebacteria, dermatophytes, Staph/Strep). Risk: obesity, diabetes, hyperhidrosis, immobility, incontinence, tight synthetics, hot/humid environments. Infant napkin dermatitis is a related fold problem.

ul: Skin-on-skin friction, trapped sweat, maceration, and alkaline irritants (urine, faeces).
**"Talc keeps folds dry"**: it can clump and irritate; dry gently and use a barrier.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Folds trap heat and moisture, so the barrier **macerates** and rubs raw.

mech.t: Skin-to-skin contact traps sweat and raises temperature.
mech.caption: Inside a skin fold: trapped moisture and friction break down the barrier.

mech.t: Wet stratum corneum softens and erodes with movement.
Damaged skin is colonised by *Candida*, dermatophytes, *Corynebacterium* (erythrasma) or streptococci.
Submammary, axillary, inguinal, abdominal and interdigital folds.
mech.caption: Common intertrigo sites.

sections.title: Clinical features

ul: Erythema, itch/burn, moist/macerated skin, fissures in crease depth, peeling.
Sites: inframammary, axillae, groin, abdominal apron, natal cleft, neck, finger/toe webs.

**Worked case:** 50-year-old; 3-month itchy red **symmetrical inframammary** rash; smooth surface, well-defined borders, mild peripheral scale; **KOH negative**; on HRT; no other sites or new topicals → diagnosis **intertrigo** (inflammatory/irritant-predominant).

blocks: Secondary infection clues: satellite pustules (candida), foul odour (Gram-negatives), honey crusts (impetigo), coral-red Wood lamp (erythrasma).

variants.name: Candida
variants.t: Beefy red with satellite papules / pustules. *Site: Folds.*

variants.name: Tinea cruris
variants.t: Raised active border, central clearing; often asymmetrical. *Site: Groin.*

variants.name: Erythrasma
variants.t: Red-brown patch, little scale or itch. *Site: Axilla, groin.*

variants.name: Seborrhoeic
variants.t: Ill-defined salmon-pink; check scalp and face. *Site: Axilla.*

variants.name: Hailey–Hailey
variants.t: Painful erosions, fissures; familial: refer. *Site: Axilla, groin.*

sub: Erythema may look brown or purple; post-inflammatory pigmentation is common.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Clinical. KOH/mycology if scale, satellites, or treatment failure; bacterial swab if pustules/crust/odour; consider patch testing if allergen suspected; biopsy if atypical or refractory (granular parakeratosis, Hailey–Hailey, etc.).

ul: Most are clinical.
If scale, satellites or treatment failure.
Swab if pustules, crust, odour; Wood’s lamp for erythrasma.
Atypical, one fold that won’t clear, or suspected allergy.

sections.title: Differential diagnoses

ddx.name: Inverse psoriasis
ddx.f: Shiny, well-demarcated; relapses as treatment stops.

ddx.name: Extramammary Paget
ddx.f: One fold that fails to clear in an older adult: biopsy.

blocks: A KOH-negative picture still overlaps early inverse psoriasis and seborrhoeic dermatitis — reassess if not settling with dry-care + mild steroid.
Key takeaway: when treating flexural rashes, **keep dry**, address incontinence/sweating/obesity, and **screen secondary bacterial/fungal infection**.

sections.title: Management

ul: Shower after sweating; **dry folds thoroughly** (cool hairdryer useful under breasts/axillae).
Loose natural-fibre clothing; address incontinence and obesity where relevant.
Barrier pastes (e.g. zinc oxide) for weepy irritant folds; avoid irritating talc as primary strategy.
Mild topical corticosteroid short course (e.g. **hydrocortisone 1%** 1–2 weeks) for inflammatory intertrigo once infection unlikely/treated.
If candida likely or empiric after failed dry-care: topical azole (± mild steroid combo products used cautiously in primary care).
Bacterial secondary infection: topical or oral antibiotic per local guidance.
Avoid potent/very potent steroids in folds (atrophy, striae, rebound).

blocks: Further management: follow-up response; if persists → repeat mycology/culture; reconsider inverse psoriasis, contact allergy, seborrhoeic dermatitis; review HRT/medications only if clinically relevant contributors.

ladder.t: Shower after sweating; **dry folds thoroughly** (cool hairdryer). Loose natural fibres; address incontinence and weight.
**Hydrocortisone 1%**, 1–2 weeks, once infection unlikely or treated.
Candida likely: topical azole (± mild steroid combo, used cautiously). Bacterial: topical or oral antibiotic per local guidance.
Repeat mycology / culture; rethink inverse psoriasis, contact allergy, seborrhoeic dermatitis.

blocks.title: Prescribing limits and pitfalls
list: **Potent steroids in folds**: Atrophy, striae and rebound: avoid.
**Combo creams**: Pragmatic, but reassess if no infection signs and no improvement.

refer.t: Single fold that won’t clear, especially older adult: biopsy for **extramammary Paget**.
Relapses as soon as treatment stops: think **inverse psoriasis**.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Rash that fails to clear in one fold, especially in an older adult: biopsy for **extramammary Paget disease**.
Spreading redness, pain and fever: cellulitis.
Repeated ‘intertrigo’ that relapses as soon as treatment stops: think **inverse psoriasis** (see the [psoriasis](condition:psoriasis) page).
Secondary infection, fissuring, odour, pain; cellulitis in diabetes.
Recurs unless predisposing factors are managed.

pearls: KOH negative ≠ “never fungal” — sampling error and mixed pictures exist; re-test if course atypical.
Combination clotrimazole–HC / similar: pragmatic in primary care but reassess if no clear infection signs and no improvement.
Counsel that **prevention** (dryness) beats endless cream cycles.

quiz.q: First step for KOH-negative irritant intertrigo?
quiz.a: Dry-care and friction reduction, plus a short course of hydrocortisone 1%.

quiz.q: Why avoid potent steroids in folds?
quiz.a: Natural occlusion increases absorption: atrophy, striae, rebound.

quiz.q: One fold that never clears in an older woman?
quiz.a: Biopsy to exclude extramammary Paget disease.
